title: Medical-Surgical Nursing II
description: Nursing management of neurological, renal and urinary, endocrine and metabolic, gastrointestinal and hepatic, and musculoskeletal conditions and burns.

topics.title: Neurological Nursing
topics.summary: Neurological observations, raised intracranial pressure, stroke care, seizures and spinal injury.

notes.b: Neurological observations include the Glasgow Coma Scale (eye opening 1–4, verbal response 1–5, motor response 1–6; total 3–15; ≤ 8 indicates coma and need for airway protection), pupil size and reaction, limb power, and vital signs. Signs of raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting, falling GCS, papilloedema, and the late Cushing's triad (hypertension with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respiration); a unilateral fixed dilated pupil suggests herniation. Nursing measures: head elevation 30°, neutral neck alignment, avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia, control fever and seizures, avoid fluid overload, and give osmotherapy (mannitol) as prescribed.

Stroke: recognise with FAST (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to seek help); CT distinguishes ischaemic from haemorrhagic stroke. Nursing: airway, swallowing assessment before oral intake (aspiration pneumonia risk), positioning and turning, early mobilisation, pressure-area care, bladder and bowel care, BP management, prevention of DVT, and rehabilitation with physiotherapy and speech therapy. Seizures: protect from injury, time the seizure, recovery position after, never restrain or put objects in the mouth; status epilepticus (> 5 minutes) needs benzodiazepines. Spinal cord injury: immobilise and log-roll; watch for respiratory compromise (high cervical injuries), neurogenic shock (hypotension with bradycardia), autonomic dysreflexia (in lesions above T6 — severe hypertension triggered by a full bladder or constipation), pressure ulcers and urinary retention.

topics.title: Renal and Urinary Nursing
topics.summary: Acute kidney injury and CKD care, dialysis, urinary catheter care and urinary tract infection.

notes.b: Nursing in acute kidney injury: accurate fluid balance and daily weights, monitoring urine output (catheterise if needed), vital signs, electrolytes (especially potassium — watch for hyperkalaemia), avoiding nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast), and recognising fluid overload. Chronic kidney disease: control BP and diabetes, dietary advice (restrict salt, potassium, phosphate and fluid as advised), anaemia management (erythropoietin, iron), vaccination (hepatitis B), and psychological support. Haemodialysis via an arteriovenous fistula — protect the fistula arm: no BP measurements, venepuncture or tight clothing; check for thrill and bruit daily. Peritoneal dialysis requires strict aseptic technique to prevent peritonitis (cloudy effluent is a warning sign).
k: Protect AV fistula arm; check thrill

notes.b: Urinary catheterisation should be performed only when necessary, with aseptic technique, closed drainage system, the bag kept below bladder level and off the floor, and daily review of the need for the catheter (catheter-associated UTI is one of the commonest hospital infections). Urinary tract infection: symptoms of frequency, urgency, dysuria and suprapubic pain (cystitis), or fever, loin pain and rigors (pyelonephritis); obtain a midstream urine for culture before antibiotics; encourage fluids. Benign prostatic hyperplasia causes lower urinary tract symptoms and retention in older men; post-prostatectomy care includes continuous bladder irrigation, monitoring for clots and bleeding, and catheter care.

topics.title: Endocrine and Metabolic Nursing
topics.summary: Diabetes care, DKA and hypoglycaemia, diabetic foot, and thyroid disorders.

notes.b: Diabetes education includes diet, exercise, medication (insulin technique and storage, oral agents), self-monitoring of blood glucose, recognising and treating hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia, sick-day rules and foot care. Diabetic ketoacidosis (usually type 1): hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia/ketonuria, metabolic acidosis, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath; nursing care involves fluid resuscitation (normal saline), IV insulin infusion, hourly glucose and regular potassium monitoring (potassium falls with insulin — replace), fluid balance and neurological observations. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state occurs in type 2 diabetes with severe dehydration. Hypoglycaemia (< 4 mmol/L): fast-acting glucose if conscious; IV dextrose or IM glucagon if not.
k: DKA: fluids, IV insulin, potassium replacement
Hypoglycaemia: glucose if conscious; IV dextrose/glucagon if not

notes.b: Diabetic foot ulcers result from neuropathy, ischaemia and infection and are a leading cause of amputation in Nigeria. Prevention: daily foot inspection (use a mirror), washing and drying between toes, moisturising (not between toes), cutting nails straight, never walking barefoot, well-fitting footwear, and prompt attention to injuries; avoid hot water bottles and home 'surgery' on corns. Thyroid: hypothyroidism — fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance; lifelong levothyroxine. Hyperthyroidism — weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia; antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or surgery. After thyroidectomy, monitor for haemorrhage (neck swelling, stridor — keep suture removal equipment at the bedside), hypocalcaemia (tingling, tetany — parathyroid damage) and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarseness); thyroid storm is an emergency.

topics.title: Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Nursing
topics.summary: GI bleeding, bowel surgery and stoma care, liver disease, and nasogastric tube care.

notes.b: Upper GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena) from peptic ulcers or oesophageal varices: assess for shock, insert large-bore cannulae, send blood for grouping and cross-match, keep nil by mouth, monitor vital signs and output, and prepare for endoscopy; give PPIs, and for variceal bleeding, vasoactive drugs (terlipressin/octreotide) and antibiotics as prescribed. Intestinal obstruction: nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression ('drip and suck'), IV fluids, monitoring. Stoma care after colostomy or ileostomy: observe stoma colour (healthy stoma is pink/red and moist; dusky or black suggests ischaemia), measure and fit appliances correctly, protect peristomal skin, monitor output (ileostomy output is liquid and high — risk of dehydration), and provide psychological support and teaching. Typhoid perforation and appendicitis are common surgical emergencies in Nigeria.
k: Upper GI bleed: resuscitate, cross-match, NBM

notes.b: Liver cirrhosis (hepatitis B and C, alcohol) causes ascites, jaundice, bleeding tendency and hepatic encephalopathy. Nursing care: monitor weight and abdominal girth, fluid and salt restriction as prescribed, diuretics (spironolactone), care during paracentesis, lactulose to reduce ammonia (aim for 2–3 soft stools daily), avoid sedatives, observe for confusion and bleeding, and nutritional support. Hepatitis B is highly prevalent in Nigeria — staff vaccination and standard precautions are essential. Nasogastric tube care: confirm position before use (aspirate pH ≤ 5.5 or X-ray), keep the head elevated during feeds, flush tubes, and monitor for aspiration and tube displacement.

topics.title: Musculoskeletal Nursing and Burns
topics.summary: Fracture care, traction and casts, compartment syndrome, and burns assessment and management.

notes.b: Fracture care: immobilisation (splints, casts, traction, internal or external fixation), pain control and neurovascular observations of the limb — the 5 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis) plus capillary refill and swelling. Compartment syndrome (raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment, e.g. after tibial fractures or tight casts) presents with pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretching — an emergency requiring release of dressings/casts and urgent fasciotomy. Cast care: keep dry, elevate the limb, do not insert objects under the cast, report tightness or odour. Traction: maintain alignment, weights hanging freely, pin-site care (external fixators). Complications of immobility: DVT, pressure ulcers, chest infection, constipation. Traditional bone setters are widely used in Nigeria and can cause complications such as limb gangrene from tight splints.
k: Compartment syndrome: pain on passive stretch → fasciotomy

notes.b: Burns are assessed by depth (superficial/epidermal, partial thickness, full thickness — painless, leathery, white or charred) and extent as % total body surface area (TBSA) using the Rule of Nines in adults (head 9%, each arm 9%, front of trunk 18%, back 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1%) or the patient's palm (≈ 1% TBSA) for small burns; children have relatively larger heads (Lund and Browder chart). First aid: stop the burning, cool with running water for 20 minutes, cover with cling film. Adults with > 15% TBSA (children > 10%) need IV fluids: the Parkland formula — 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA of Ringer's lactate over 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from the time of injury. Monitor urine output (0.5 mL/kg/h in adults; 1 mL/kg/h in children). Watch for airway burns (singed nasal hair, hoarseness, soot — early intubation), infection, and contractures (splinting, physiotherapy). Kerosene and gas explosions and cooking accidents are common causes in Nigeria.
k: Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA; half in 8 h
